_note: Short concept notes used for L0 hints and concept cards. Examples deliberately use other names and widths than the problems, so they teach without solving.

module_ports.title: Modules and ports
module_ports.note: A module is a box with named inputs and outputs. Everything you build lives between `module` and `endmodule`, and the port list says what goes in and out.

assign.title: Continuous assignment
assign.note: `assign` connects a wire to an expression permanently. It is a physical connection, not a one-time copy: whenever the right side changes, the left side follows.

multi_assign.title: Several outputs
multi_assign.note: Each output needs its own driver. Write one `assign` per output; their order does not matter because they all act at the same time.
multi_assign.example:
assign p = m;
assign q = n;

bitwise_ops.title: Gates as operators
bitwise_ops.note: `~` is NOT, `&` is AND, `|` is OR, `^` is XOR. NOR, NAND and XNOR are a gate followed by `~`, for example `~(m | n)`.

internal_wire.title: Internal wires
internal_wire.note: Declare a `wire` to name an intermediate signal inside the module. It is not a port, so the outside world never sees it, but it makes larger circuits readable.

vector_decl.title: Declaring vectors
vector_decl.note: `[7:0]` declares 8 bits numbered 7 down to 0. The first number is the most significant bit. Declaring `[0:7]` reverses which end is bit 0.
vector_decl.example: wire [3:0] nibble;   // nibble[3] is the MSB

part_select.title: Selecting bits
part_select.note: `v[3]` picks one bit and `v[7:4]` picks a range. Count carefully: `v[7:4]` is 4 bits, and the indices must stay inside the declared range.

bitwise_vs_logical.title: Bitwise versus logical
bitwise_vs_logical.note: `|` works bit by bit and keeps the width. `||` asks whether either side is non-zero and returns a single bit. On multi-bit vectors they give different answers.

multi_input_gates.title: Wide gates
multi_input_gates.note: A gate with many inputs is the operator applied across all of them. A reduction operator such as `&v` ANDs every bit of `v` together.
multi_input_gates.example: assign all_ones = &flags;   // AND of every bit

concat.title: Concatenation
concat.note: `{p, q}` glues signals side by side. The first item becomes the most significant bits. Concatenation also works on the left side of an assignment.
concat.example:
assign packed = {hi_byte, lo_byte};
assign {carry, total} = m + n;

reversal.title: Reversing bit order
reversal.note: Reversing means bit 0 goes to the top and the top bit goes to bit 0. With few bits, a concatenation of single bits in the opposite order does it.

replication.title: Replication
replication.note: `{N{x}}` repeats `x` N times. It is the clean way to make a wide signal from one bit. A 1-bit signal used with a 32-bit one is otherwise padded with zeros, not copied.

sign_extend.title: Sign extension
sign_extend.note: To widen a signed number, copy its top bit into the new upper bits. Filling with zeros turns negative numbers into large positive ones.

instantiation.title: Using another module
instantiation.note: Instantiating a module places a copy of it in your circuit: write the module name, a name for this copy, then the connections.

port_by_position.title: Connecting by position
port_by_position.note: Without names, connections are matched to ports in the order the module declares them. Check the declaration order, not the order you would like.
port_by_position.example:
// declared as: module box(output o, input i1, input i2);
box b0 (y, m, n);

port_by_name.title: Connecting by name
port_by_name.note: `.port(signal)` connects by name, so order no longer matters. It is safer and easier to read than positional connections.

chaining.title: Chaining modules
chaining.note: The output of one instance can feed the input of the next through an internal wire. Each flip-flop in a chain adds one clock cycle of delay.

mux.title: Choosing with a multiplexer
mux.note: A multiplexer passes one of several inputs depending on a select signal. The `? :` operator is a 2-to-1 mux; a `case` statement handles more inputs.

carry_chain.title: Carry chain
carry_chain.note: When adding wide numbers in pieces, the carry-out of the lower piece must become the carry-in of the next one. The lowest carry-in is 0 for plain addition.

full_adder.title: Full adder
full_adder.note: A full adder adds three bits: two inputs and a carry-in. It produces a sum bit and a carry-out. The sum is the XOR of all three; the carry is 1 when at least two inputs are 1.

carry_select.title: Carry-select adder
carry_select.note: To avoid waiting for the low carry, compute the high half twice, once assuming carry-in 0 and once assuming 1, then pick the right result when the real carry arrives.

add_sub.title: Subtracting with an adder
add_sub.note: In two's complement, m - n equals m + ~n + 1. An adder can therefore subtract if you invert n and set the carry-in to 1 when subtracting.
